payload.description_html:
Chasmosaurus belli (Lambe, 1902) - fossil ceratopsian dinosaur skull from the Cretaceous of Montana, USA. (Ronald Ruschman collection)

Ceratopsians are the "horned dinosaurs". They were large, quadrupedal, herbivorous dinosaurs having a beaked skull and a frill - an extension of bone behind the skull that partially covered the neck. Ceratopsian dinosaurs are known from the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The last members of the group died out at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary, 65 million years ago.

Chasmosaurus belli was a ceratopsian having three horns on the face - one over the snout and two over the eyes. The frill has many short, marginal bony knobs and two large fenestra, which are openings in the bone. Fenestra functioned to keep down the weight of the skull.

In the skull shown above, the apparent right-angle relationship between the horizontal plane of the skull and the long axis of the frill is an artifact caused by post-depositional compression. During life, the frill extended behind the skull at a moderately low angle to the horizontal.

Classification: Animalia, Chordata, Vertebrata, Reptilia, Archosauria, Dinosauria, Ornithischia, Marginocephalia, Ceratopsia, Ceratopsidae

Stratigraphy: Judith River Formation, Campanian Stage, upper Upper Cretaceous

Locality: unrecorded/undisclosed site near the town of Havre, northern Montana, USA.
